utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a problem with the audio system. We will have to adjourn for five minutes. We will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.07 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, how long can you remain with us today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As long as necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. What we'll do is this: We will sit for two sessions today; an hour and a half, and then we'll take a break, and then another hour and a half. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know anything about the infiltration of foreign terrorists in Kosovo? For example, terrorists of Al Qaeda? That was my last question, in fact. And you said that you had no knowledge of that. That was where we left off. And among other things, you said that in Malisevo in July, you saw only one possible individual from the Middle East but that you saw no further evidence of Al Qaeda activities or any other terrorist organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in Malisevo at that time, did you ask the leaders of that terrorist group, the KLA, who the man was you saw amongst them whom you assumed was a terrorist from the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did ask various people, but they were not willing to tell me who he was, and so I left it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they -- did you ask them what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was fairly obvious what he was doing there. He was part of the disparate group involved with the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement and the part relating to Malisevo, I don't see that you informed your government about that. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Mr. Milosevic, it is not written in the statement that I informed my government, but I did actually make mention of it during my other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you this: Do you have any information as to the following - and I'm going to quote briefly a passage from the interview before the Committee for International Relations of Congress - it is dated October, the 3rd of October, 2001, and it was a presentation made by Winston Kalistrala [phoen], the former head of the counter-terrorist operation, CIA group. And he says that bin Laden was against his own monarchy in Saudi Arabia, that he was expelled by their service there and that he went to the Sudan where he organised camps, training camps, for Islamic activists and for practically all the major Islamic countries. And the quotation is as follows -- I'm going to ask you whether you had knowledge of any of this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment. I see that nobody in the public gallery is getting the sound, is able to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going on with the trial. That's simply a matter for the public. Let's go on. The witness, I think, knows nothing about this anyway. This is somebody giving evidence to the Senate International Relations Committee in October 2001. Do you know anything about bin Laden in Bosnia -- or in Kosovo, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said, Your Honour, the only possible person was this one person I saw in Malisevo. I don't have any knowledge of this document that Mr. Milosevic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you saw the document. That's not the essential point. I wish to read out what it says here for you to be able to respond and tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, there's no point putting something to him about which he knows nothing. A great deal of time is spent in this trial with your reading out documents and things about which the witnesses know nothing at all. So move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I assume that the British intelligence service has knowledge of the role of Al Qaeda. And if it did not have any knowledge in 1998, I'm sure that after the 11th of September, it did have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got the answer. He doesn't know, apart from the man in Malisevo. Now, that's the end of it. If you want to put that evidence before us, you can call the man who gave evidence to the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know this: That at a national symposium on drug terrorism on the 4th of December, 2001, among other things, it was noted that there were links between drug trafficking and terrorist organisations and that it is maintained that those links are very well documented. And of course, mention is made there of the KLA and others; Chechena and other radical groups. Are you aware of that? You have that, for example, on the 4th of December, 2001. That's when that took place. The Justice Ministry. Drug enforcement administration. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think everyone knows that terrorist organisations are involved in drug and Mafia trafficking. I don't really see what this has got to do with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it does have something to do with it because the Albanian drug Mafia are the main smugglers of drugs. And it also is connected because it financed terrorist organisations which were infiltrated from outside into Kosovo and that's why I'm asking you whether you know anything about that. And is it possible that your service knows nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that my service or the British government intelligence services knows nothing about the drug trafficking. Of course they know about that. You will also be well aware that there was a lot of drug trafficking that went on in Belgrade. I presume your service knew also about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our services very often arrested members of terrorist groups for the most part and seized the goods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to waste time on this. Now, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In answering questions during the examination-in-chief with respect to Racak, you said that you were in Racak on the 15th of January and that you had arrived there sometime around 1400 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is correct, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You maintain that you saw that the village of Racak had been shelled by the police and army. Tell me now, please, how many houses were destroyed or damaged in Racak? Did you see any damaged or destroyed houses in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, the majority of the houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you have any knowledge as to how many inhabitants of Racak were killed or wounded by those shells that were allegedly launched on the village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if I remember rightly, something like 31 to 35 bodies were brought out of Racak after that operation, but I can't remember exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. Do you know that not a single person, a single individual who lost their lives in the fighting around Racak was not killed by shrapnel or shelling or grenades but exclusively from the fire of infantry weapons? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, how is it possible, Mr. Crosland, then, for the MUP and the army to keep shelling Racak without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his explanation. He's told us what he saw. It's not for him to speculate. It will be a matter which we will have to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Crosland, I noticed you said that 35 bodies were brought out, and also I noticed the 10th of July, when you firstly gave evidence, you also mentioned some seven or eight bodies of KLA members were brought out. Could you clarify "bring out the bodies"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I remember, in a gully close to this village called Racak, approximately 30 bodies were found. And again, I believe seven or eight were possibly from the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you use the term "being brought out" as meaning found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I believe they were found in this gully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By Ambassador Walker and other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that from 1400 hours onwards, you were there and that you were there in the throes of heavy fighting. Do you know that after 1400 hours, when the fighting had already stopped, the police withdrew and that the local commander of the KLA here testified that at 1600 hours they had already taken control of the village again? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can -- I'm sorry to interrupt but the witness can only tell us what he saw or heard while he was there, and he's given his evidence. Now, it's for you in due course to address us on it, if you wish. If you want to suggest, of course, that there was no fighting and that the witness is wrong, you can do so, if that's your case. But there's no point in reading out things that other people have said. He can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not reading out at all what other people said, Mr. May. All I'm doing is placing the statement of this witness in a relationship with the facts that were ascertained here, and that is that on the 15th, around 1500 hours, the operation was already over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to allow this. This is not the time for comment, as you know well, or speeches. Colonel, it seems to be suggested, or in case it's being suggested that you're wrong and there was no fighting at 2.00 when you arrived, can you give us, please, your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fighting had more or less subsided by about 2.00 in the afternoon. That and the -- what Mr. Milosevic is saying, that the KLA possibly had retaken possession of the village by 4.00, 1600, I think happened time after time after time within the province of Kosovo. That rather pointed to the futility of a lot of the Serbian security operations that nothing had been achieved by destroying their villages. A tactic that had been employed by the Serbian security forces is at the basis of what this investigation is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness in fact said, according to my note, was this: That he arrived just after the main conflict but there was still activity going on, and covering fire was being provided into Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm claiming, that at the time the witness arrived and that he says he watched the conflict, that the conflict had in fact been over by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said you saw members of the Verification Mission, and you said that during your examination-in-chief as well. So in Racak, on the 15th of January. And your answer was that you had seen them and that you believe you saw Ambassador Walker as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when asked whether you were there when the conflict was going on, you said yes, because you were there when the main conflict began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that. I've just read out my note of what he said. He arrived just after the main conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7949, that page of the transcript, Mr. May. There you have it. Your own transcript of Wednesday, the LiveNote on Wednesday. The question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see members of the Kosovo Verification Mission [in English] while you were there? The answer was:

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did [Previous translation continues]... [in English] Ambassador Walker but I can't remember precisely. Perhaps you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you there when the actual conflict occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived just after the major conflict had arrived, but there was considerable activity ongoing that afternoon and throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not disputed that he said it. Now, can we move on to some more relevant point? What is the point you're trying to make with him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely the opposite from what you said a moment ago, that he didn't say it, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are not going to waste further time on this. I've read you out my note which coincides with what the transcript said. There's no point arguing about it. Now, have you got any more questions for him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me this -- yes, I have many more questions. I've just started my cross-examination, Mr. May, and I don't know why you ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you exactly see William Walker in Racak? What time was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I told you, I arrived about 2.00 in the afternoon and, as far as I can recall, I remember seeing Mr. Walker sometime during the afternoon period. This was a highly fluid and difficult area where operations were still going on and people were coming and going throughout the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you talk to him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to him on that occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me where you were on the 14th of January. That is to say, on the eve of the events in Racak.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think I was in Belgrade, having just returned to Belgrade from the United Kingdom. I was preparing to come down to Kosovo the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, about the events in Racak, as you were there on the 15th of January, did you draw up a report of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent -- there's a written report, as I think has been explained to you, and I used to be in communication by other means back to both Belgrade and to the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me why, then, this report was not included with all the other reports that you have presented here, as Racak is an essential event.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you when I was in court last week, Mr. Milosevic, I didn't choose the reports. It was chosen by other people. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You want to say that you gave them all 70 of your reports and that they selected the several reports that were presented; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reports were the -- or are the -- in the keeping of the Ministry of Defence in the United Kingdom, and which reports are passed across to this court, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the killing of three Serb policemen and the conflict and clash between the police force and the Ahmeti group on the 28th of February, 1998. Were you present when this police operation was waged?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean -- which operation do you mean, when the three MUP were killed or when the operation took place at Likosane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when the operation took place on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one was present because the whole area was sealed off. I was touring with another defence attache and we came in shortly after we were allowed through. That particular area was sealed for a number of days by your security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge that on that occasion there was fighting between the terrorists and the forces -- the security forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have knowledge that there was fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were those people killed in battle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I wasn't there. All I know is that 26 people were buried north of Likosane a couple of days later, as witnessed by the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On Wednesday, you said that 16 persons were killed, that 16 of them were killed in that operation. Now, this 26 now, does that mean that somebody from other operations who had lost their lives were buried or what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The information was that these 16 had been killed in Likosane or around that area, and the further ten were seen being taken alive, we believe to Prizren -- sorry, to Pristina, beg your pardon, and were returned dead. You will have to or someone will have to answer that question; I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you suggesting -- are you suggesting that somebody took the people to the prison, killed them there, and brought them back dead?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the suggestion, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come such a - how shall I put it? - drastic event is not mentioned in your reports, that somebody took off the prisoners, killed them, and brought them back dead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is. It's mentioned in the statement which I've got in front of me. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: I understood that you were in Donje Prekaze when the fighting was going on there. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not in Donje Prekaze when the fighting was going on because the whole area was closed down. I was probably the first person into Donje Prekaze directly after the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you weren't there actually when it all went on. You weren't present.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about the fact that the members of the Ministry of the Interior on several occasions before they opened fire called out to the group of terrorists led by Jashari to surrender?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that from various sources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that when they didn't want to surrender, that they asked them to let the women and children leave, to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know for which major crimes, and I'm thinking about numerous killings, Adem Jashari was prosecuted for, and the other members of his group?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the details, Mr. Milosevic, no. I know he had -- there was indications that he had been involved in various activities, yes. But I don't see, you know, this is what is leading to the very deliberate and totally destructive attack that took place on Donje Prekaze which involved armoured vehicles firing at 30 metres. I think that explains the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, an Albanian who was a protected witness here talked about what happened, and this completely coincides with what I myself am saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to, and in fact you can't ask this witness to comment on what some other witness has said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, then: Who gave you access to that locality and allowed you to tour the spot after this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the MUP or the PJP commander in charge in Srbica allowed us in, and we photographed the bodies that were at the southern entrance to Srbica in a low, one-storey house just on the southern entrance to Srbica. And there were, I think, as I've said in my statement, 54 bodies; men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, paragraph 4, you claim that during that period of time there were a series of KLA attacks against the police force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many such attacks took place in the course of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to be updated by your General Staff on the number of attacks, and I can't remember the details now. But I'm not disputing the fact that there were attacks. I'm disputing the fact that the actions carried out by your security forces really did very little to restore the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether they helped or not, do you realise that at the end of 1998, the facts say that to all practical intents and purposes the KLA was not capable of launching any more operations at all, that they had been totally neutralised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Milosevic, I'm not certain that's correct, because within -- if I remember rightly, between October and November, whilst your forces had gained the initiative in the early part of the autumn, the Kosovo Liberation Army did get or appeared to receive new supplies. I don't think I've, you know, been in dispute with you that there is, there was and has been a terrorist problem within Kosovo. What I am suggesting is that the way your tactics carried out, as has now been proved, is actually highly unsuccessful and that the burning and destroying of villages - sometimes several times over; crops, petrol stations, the workshops, all the other infrastructure of life - has done nothing actually to help the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about something else now. In the autumn of 1998, since you were there, I believe that you remember well that the situation had calmed down, that they even brought weapons in on tractors and handed them in. The security situation was almost completely restored to normal, and then, practically, there was a new stage when the Kosovo Verification Mission came. Regardless of whether you want to confirm this or not, they saved the KLA. Is that right or is that not right? They made it possible for the KLA to be revitalised. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to answer a question yes or no of that magnitude is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Without yes or no, perhaps you could comment on it if you think you can, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the arrival of the Kosovo Verification Mission was a part of the process of attempting to bring this troubled area to peace. To blame them for an uprise in the KLA, I think is grossly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see, the commander of the KLA, Ramush Haradinaj -- there's even a book that was published, I can give it to you as a present, in English, he says: " [Previous translation continues]... [In English] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saving for KLA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's his comment. You can tell us about it in due course. Now, do let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since frequent meetings are referred to here with the representatives of the British, American, French, Canadian, et cetera, as he says here, missions, KDOM, et cetera, and then it says: [Previous translation continues]... [In English] in itself of NATO airstrikes that would follow later on." [Interpretation] Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are you reading from? Where are you reading from in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the book, Ramush Haradinaj's book. The book of commander Ramush Haradinaj. And after the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Move on to ask him some questions about his evidence or about his statement, not the opinions of people in books.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not opinion, Mr. May. I'm asking him whether they helped the KLA recover, and did they, with the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer: "No." Now, you must learn not to argue with the witnesses. You have to accept their evidence. You can argue the case to us in due course, but there's no point arguing with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I never argue with witnesses. As far as I can see, it's you who's arguing with me all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crosland, do you know that in 1998, 1.854 terrorist attacks were carried out by the KLA in Kosovo and Metohija? That is approximately more than four per day, on average. However, the number went up after the Verification Mission arrived, considerably so. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said to you, Mr. Milosevic, we used to get -- or I used to get fairly regular briefings from your General Staff, General Dimitrijevic and other people, and that figure would have been given to me. But let's put it into context with other operations and other areas that I've been involved in. Of course the security forces will document every single minor action that the opposite side does in order to build up their own statistics, but I don't really see where this leads us. I was fully aware that there was a serious situation developing in Kosovo, as I've said to you and I put in my reports, and I reported this accurately on both sides. I don't really know what else I could do. I could not influence the situation apart from report it both back to your Vojska Yugoslavia General Staff in Belgrade and to my authorities back in the United Kingdom. That is clearly documented in all my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it uncontested that the objectives of the attack, or rather, the targets were the members of the Ministry of the Interior, the members of the military but civilians as well, both Serbs and Albanians and Muslims and members of other ethnic communities in Kosovo? They were killed, they were kidnapped, they were robbed, et cetera. Do you know about that or did you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I knew about that. But you must bear that in context with what your security forces were doing to something like 2 to 3 to 400 villages that I saw burned to the ground. So it's not unnatural that people took revenge. I'm afraid reconciliation in the Balkans is not a word that's very much known about, "osveta." More "osveta" and less -- a bit more "pomirenje" and less "osveta" would be a better thing all around. More reconciliation and less revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in 1998, Mr. Crosland, was there a major increase in terrorism in Kosovo? Is that being contested?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, no. I've told you that in my reports, that the situation initially started at the latter end of 1997 when I first had talks with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic and then grew in intensity during the early part of 1998. There was then a Serbian security offensive in July, August, September, which led inevitably to the Holbrooke mission. There was a relatively quiet period, but during that period, as I've already said, the Kosovo Liberation Army appeared to get more supplies into the area, then a resumption of Serbian activity -- security force activity just prior to Christmas and then with Bozic and Serbian New Year, there was a quiet-ish period in mid-January until we came to the Racak affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then this notorious Racak happened; right? And then, as you mentioned here, you presented your views to Dimitrijevic and two other generals, that they were getting involved in a long campaign with few chances of success. That's what you said. Now I'm asking you as a military man who has experience, I imagine, in fighting terrorism as well. What would a shorter campaign entail, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. May, is that this witness, as a soldier, as a professional soldier, is challenging what the police and army did in their struggle against terrorism. So I would like to hear his position, what this would look like in the organisation of his army and his police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about. It seems to me totally irrelevant. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, to what extent did your intelligence activities focus on gathering data on the KLA, its manpower, weapon levels, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, within the Kosovo region, I reported back on the KLA that one saw and their activities as is laid out in those reports or other reports that you may not have seen, I don't know. As far as externally, that is the duties of various UK services of which I was not a part of, as you well know. I was accredited to your -- to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 4, in paragraph 5, you mention that the MUP forces were sufficient to deal with an average rebellion. The question is whether keeping 50 per cent of the territory under terrorist control is something that you consider to be an average rebellion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if you're referring to the situation in the middle of the -- the early part of the summer in Kosovo and Metohija, I spoke with several of your senior staff and queried as to why they were allowing the Kosovo Liberation Army to control, I think it was three of the major roads across Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is correct, of course. These three main routes that are a precondition for life in Kosovo and Metohija were blocked in certain places by the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- [Previous translation continues]... Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- yes. What you were going to say, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Milosevic. And I used to travel this area on more or less a daily basis, and these positions, these KLA positions, were not of any great strength or depth, could not have been attacked? That is the question you must ask your security forces. As I've referred to, this is a question of tactics. If your security forces had concentrated on purely the Kosovo Liberation Army defensive positions, I don't think there would have been a problem. But when they went into villages to destroy villages for no other reason than they wished to take these villages down - and the excuse I was given was that it provides cover along the routes - I don't find that very convincing when some of these routes were completely irrelevant to the operations. Major routes were blocked, the wooded area in the central part of Kosovo, which although quite difficult to operate in was by no means impossible with the number of troops that your forces had deployed on the ground against, I would suggest, probably in the early part of 1998, my ‘guesstimate’ or -- of the numbers of the KLA was probably about 3 to 400 hard-core at the very most. So not a great deal of people. But I can't answer the question why your forces did not use the tactics to clear these people out of what were quite clearly illegal defensive positions. Even when I went through their positions and their headquarters in Malisevo, the KLA would not recognise my licna karta as defence attache to your country and I informed them that I was allowed to go anywhere I liked within the country of Yugoslavia; there was no legal rule here. I put the question back to you; it is up to your forces to have carried out the correct tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not talking about tactics here, Mr. Crosland. We are talking about crimes and the behaviour of a terrorist organisation that killed many people. Are you denying the right of the legal forces to fight terrorism?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, no. I'm actually -- as I tried to explain to the Vojska Yugoslavia General Staff, that if your forces attacked the KLA in these illegal positions, as I've already explained to you, then I don't think anyone would have had any problem. What was the problem was the total wanton destruction over half of Kosovo against a population that, yes, was mainly Albanian. But I think there is a political side to this that has not been looked at. And even the situation now, there is no military solution to Kosovo. There very rarely is a military solution. We in the military have to come along when the political side has failed to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, does it seem to you perhaps that the fact that there was a great intensity of terrorist activities and, therefore, reactions of the forces to such intensive terrorist activities is something that you have been calling systematic damage or attacks at some peaceful villages? Haven't you confused certain concepts, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, not at all. I understand perfectly well, having been involved in counter-terrorist operations, attacks on terrorists or groups of terrorists by security forces are one thing, and that is pure military business. But for troops or security forces to go around razing, looting, burning crops, houses and businesses is not part of a proper military operation. This is just wanton destruction and revenge against, in the majority, innocent people. Of course I'm not, you know, saying that there was not support in the villages because these people are Albanians. There was probably nearly 2 million Albanians living in Kosovo. They undoubtedly had some support. Can you not see that if you go and burn and loot most of the villages in central Kosovo, who are just pure farmers and people doing their job of work --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Crosland. Please answer my questions. Do you know that many houses in Kosovo, and perhaps even entire settlements like the Prilep you mentioned, were used as fortifications and KLA terrorists operated from there against the army, against the police? They blocked roads, they made normal life impossible, they committed numerous crimes. So do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? Colonel Crosland, you're being asked about the use of settlements such as Prilep as fortifications which were used for operations against the police and the rest of it. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, within the area of Prilep there was, yes, a Kosovo Liberation Army area of operations. The point I am making, Your Honour, is that the major town of Decani, which is an old and interesting town with Visoki Decani, one of the great monasteries of Serbia, the entire Albanian area within that town was systematically burnt out as a revenge. And my point is: What does this revenge achieve? It achieves nothing. Kosovo is now under NATO control with the Albanians. Does that mean you've had a successful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Colonel, you too could restrict your answers. Time is limited. You say that within the area of Prilep there were KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were scattered within several areas of Kosovo, areas that were semi-controlled by the Kosovo Liberation Army, of which I knew about and of which I reported back on. And we get back to the same old thing about the tactics employed, yes, by both sides, I would accept that. But you don't -- if you fight terrorism with civilian terrorism, i.e., going around razing villages, all you do is drive more people to support the terrorists. It's as simple as that. I don't condone terrorism. I never will and never have. But the heavy-handed and wanton destruction in the majority of innocent areas and the crops and all the associated infrastructure can only push more people to fight against your forces. I think that is what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, let us clarify this situation. You said that 50 per cent of the territory was held by the members of the KLA for a while. You're talking about fighting all over Kosovo. You're talking about the damage done, about the victims, et cetera. Please give me a precise answer to this question: Was this area -- were these areas under long and heavy fighting between the Ministry of the Interior and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was -- Mr. Milosevic, there was a period in early 1998, after the two assaults on to Likosane and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you said "No" by way of an answer, so let's go on, Mr. Crosland. So there was not protracted and heavy fighting in that area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. The question was: Was there an area under protected and heavy fighting, and you began to answer, Colonel Crosland. Now, could you complete your answer. You started with a period in early 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that initial period at Prekaze and Likosane, there was then an area of stalemate in the early part of the summer before your forces built up. And during that time, the KLA, as I have said, controlled three of the major roads through. I say "controlled"; they sat on these routes in pretty thin defensive positions. For some reason - I can't answer that question - your forces allowed them to stay there. Now, with the amount of forces you had in Kosovo, you could have carried out operations against these defensive areas which could possibly have succeeded. For some reason, your forces did not and contented themselves with destroying the surrounding villages and all the infrastructure, which I've said on many occasions. Now, that only would have made more people join the liberation movement against your forces. And I don't understand the reason you did this. As I said, it was not a military solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can I infer, on the basis of what you've been claiming, that the security forces did not attack KLA strongholds, that they left them alone and then they went out to burn peaceful villages, to kill the livestock and damage these places? Is that what you are claiming, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm saying, Mr. Milosevic, because around the Drenica, there was something like 45 vehicle checkpoints manned by squads of men. And during this period, the Drenica was under fairly heavy attack by your forces on more or less a daily basis. Now, I can't answer the tactics and why your men did these things, I can only report to you what I saw. And as I reported back to your General Staff, I said, "I don't understand what you are trying to achieve, because you are tying more and more men up on operations that are achieving nothing and leaving them open to attacks by the Kosovo Liberation Army to what we call penny packeting, little dots here and there all over the map that really control nothing. But there was no -- if you're going to get down to tactics, there was no night patrolling by your forces and there was very little holding ground apart from what they actually saw from their defensive positions. You could see where the Kosovo Liberation Army walked up 2 or 300 metres away and then walked around the position to carry out whatever activities there were doing. And if your forces call that controlling the situation, then I'm afraid I disagree. That is the basis of my statement saying that your forces were employing the wrong type of tactics. I made this clear to various people, including General Perisic during our talks in Beograd. I had recognised, amongst other people, that there was a terrorist problem, that actually, your forces were failing to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, since you say that these were some kind of weak positions at certain places in Kosovo, that that's what the KLA did in Kosovo, so how did then these poorly armed and few members of the KLA manage, as you had claimed yourself, to control 50 per cent of the territory in spite of such well-armed and numerous troops of the military and the army, again as you have been claiming?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've already stated that they had various roadblocks across these three areas, with some supporting positions. But they were not seriously, you know, defended positions. If your forces had attacked those positions in a proper, organised manner, I'm sure they would have succeeded. Now, why they did not, I don't know. You will have to ask that question to the relevant personnel concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the most frequent targets of terrorist attacks were precisely members of the army of Yugoslavia? Did you manage to find that out during your contacts with the generals that you communicated with? You say that you noticed that there was evidence of coordination between the army and the police, the MUP, and their actions; is that right? Now, tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. You've already asked him one question, you're now going on to a second. The question was: As far as you could understand from your contacts, were the target of attacks members of the army of Yugoslavia? I don't know if you can answer that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The major attacks were against the MUP forces initially, although on the border there had been attacks against the Vojska Yugoslavia positions, particularly on the Albanian frontier. And that was well documented and evidence was produced by your General Staff, to me and other people, of these ongoing attacks. And I was well aware of the attacks on the MUP and the other security forces and of the funerals that took place back in Serbia of these people who had been killed on operations. I think throughout my time, I observed, as a military man, that when someone is killed in operations, one respects what he is doing for his country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the border of Yugoslavia only in 1998 was violated several hundreds of times through arms smuggling from Albania, transfers of well-armed and equipped groups of terrorists who were trained in camps in Northern Albania and so on? So several hundreds of times. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I do, and I explained that to you the last time I was in court, that the information initially came from your General Staff covering this area of the border between Albania, which, as you are well aware, is a historical smuggling and contraband route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. And do you consider that the army should have refrained from its basic duty to protect the state borders and to protect the populace and its members and all the facilities and communication? Is that what they should have done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has accepted that. He's accepted there was a right to do that. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this: What is there illogical in the fact that you saw that the army and MUP were cooperating? Was it logical for the police and army of one and the same state, when faced with the danger and crimes perpetrated by terrorism, should cooperate? Is that something that is not standard practice otherwise? Is that something unusual?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under your constitution, Mr. Milosevic - and I would be very careful about lecturing you about your own constitution - but the Vojska Yugoslavia had a priority to protect the national border and 500 metres. And that was written down in the constitution. As I said before, this then spread to other areas when the situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, of course that is not written down in the constitution. At least it is easy to ascertain what the constitution stipulates. But let me ask you this, because quite obviously you don't know the provisions: Do you know the law on defence, the law on the Yugoslav army? Do you know the rules of service for the army and all the rules and regulations that regulate the elements under which the army functions in all aspects and fields, let alone the constitution? That is not something that is written down in the constitution. No 500 metres or borders or whatever. Do you know about all these rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what was told to me by your foreign liaison service as part of the Ministry of Defence. Now, of course I do not know the full details. I don't know the full details of what the British army's constitution is. So to answer that in the affirmative, under oath, would be illegal. That is not the point. The point you're asking is the cooperation between the VJ and the MUP. Of course they would cooperate as the situation got worse. It's how they cooperated, by using direct and indirect fire into villages, is not part of modern way of doing -- dealing with the situation. Did it provide the right answer? The answer is quite clearly no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Crosland. This lack of information on your part as to rules and regulations probably had, as a consequence, a completely erroneous explanation for certain behaviour and conduct. But we will come to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can stop the comments and just get on with the questions. You're taking up much too much time with these lengthy questions. I will remind you, you've got now 25 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that can't be possible that I only have 25 minutes left, Mr. May, in view of the fact that I have used up very little of my time and this is a very, if I can put it that way, long, lengthy witness as to the things he is asserting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not only possible but it's the fact that you've got 25 minutes left. Two hours was what you were given. You've spent most of it arguing with the witness. Now, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's be a little more efficacious, Mr. Crosland, with the answers. On page 6 of your own statement here, you say on the 20th of August that the club of military attaches, General Ojdanic, the Deputy Chief of Staff, presented reasons for the joint operations of MUP and the army in the Malisevo area and other areas because he said that they were in keeping with one of the four assignments in Kosovo, tasks in Kosovo. And then first, the protection of communications and roads in Kosovo, maintenance of the border security, protection of the army facilities of Yugoslavia, protection of units of the army in barracks and in the field, et cetera. Now, regardless of this unwieldy interpretation of one of the four tasks or assignments, do you know, nevertheless, Mr. Crosland, that according to the rules of service of the army of Yugoslavia in peacetime Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the army of Yugoslavia can be deployed, of course, for all these tasks that you were explained to as being legitimately done by the army of Yugoslavia and also many other assignments and tasks? And I should like to mention in particular the struggle against sabotage and terrorist groups. So according to the rules of service, the rules and regulations and their provisions - and you refer to the constitution in a highly incompetent way - the Yugoslavia army, under those rules and regulations that are valid and that you can read through, can be used, may be used against sabotage and terrorist groups; it can be used to protect the communications and roads; it can be deployed for the purpose of dealing with any situations where military facilities have come under attack or the army itself has come under attack, of course in order to protect the state borders in-depth, et cetera, and so on and so forth. So where is the problem there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question you're asking? You've gone on for two minutes but we've got no question. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that there is nothing that is unlawful there in the Yugoslav army's actions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're missing the entire point. We had stated -- we had pointed out to your General Staff that it is quite clear that the Vojska Yugoslavia army was highly involved in the operations throughout the middle of 1998. It was your General Staff, Colonel General Ojdanic, who refuted it completely until I showed him a video and other evidence that this was not true. So I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, Ojdanic presented the reasons for this joint activity on the part of the army and MUP in the area of Stimlje and Malisevo, and he said -- he did not deny -- he did not deny -- you yourself said that they were in keeping and in conformity with the tasks of the army in Kosovo, and then he went on to enumerate the protection of the communication lines, ensuring the borders' security, protection of units in barracks, and otherwise. And therefore, he precisely explained the reasons for which it was completely legitimate and legal to -- and lawful to use the army and why the army's activities were lawful. And I enumerated the provisions and rules and regulations, as I said that what you had said did not exist in the constitution but I said what the rules of service for the Yugoslav army stipulate. Now, why should that be questionable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time here. The witness has already been over this. The point, Mr. Milosevic, is not whether the army should or should not have been deployed or what the constitution said or didn't say. The point of the witness's evidence was the use of artillery against the villages, undefended villages, the destruction it caused. Now, that's the point you should be concentrating on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, first of all, there were no attacks on undefended villages in Kosovo. Now, I'm asking the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether a facility or a house or a fortified village or any facility of that kind from which fire is opened on the army and police is a legitimate military target or not.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know full well that under the Geneva Conventions you are not entitled to fire artillery or anti-aircraft weapons that are specifically designed to attack aircraft at ground targets. Now, these tactics were used, as I have stated under sworn oath, throughout Kosovo against many, many villages. Both artillery, self-propelled artillery, normal towed artillery, main battle tank, including multi-rocket launching systems which were fired, I saw being fired into Junik --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I heard you. I heard you, Mr. Crosland. You said that a 20-millimetre cannon was used, is that right, anti-aircraft gun, 20-millimetre one. That's what you said was used. Now, as you're a soldier yourself, answer me this: Is there anywhere in the armaments of any army a cannon which is of smaller calibre than the 20-millimetre one? Is there a smaller calibre gun than 20 millimetres at all in the arsenal of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are many, many calibres, from 9 millimetre to 556, 762, 12.5, all the way up to 20, to 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about cannons. You're talking about artillery devices.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course a cannon cannot be under 20 millimetres. A gun, top of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is there any smaller calibre for a cannon than this 20-millimetre one? So it means that this was the smallest calibre cannon that was used for those targets that you're talking about. And secondly, it is not correct, Mr. Crosland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with the calibres, first of all, since you've raised it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the direction of your question. Various military equipments come in various calibres. Machine-guns go from 556 to 762; heavy machine-guns of 12.5. And all these were used in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the calibre of weapons now. I'm asking you a very specific question, and that is: Is there a cannon? I don't know what the interpretation was. Perhaps it was "gun." I meant cannon because gun can mean a rifle, because you said 5.6, et cetera. So cannon, is there a cannon with a smaller calibre than the 20-millimetre calibre and your answer was no, that such a cannon does not exist. Now, let's go back to more important questions, please. You're claiming, therefore, that General Dimitrijevic explained to you the fact that Pavkovic was not adhering to orders from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was General Dimitrijevic's words to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They were General Dimitrijevic's words, the ones that you're quoting here. Now, what I'm asking you is this: Do you imply and understand that it is possible, in any army whatsoever, for any event that occurs in the course of a day that a daily report should not be drafted which is then sent to the higher command, superior command? And as this was the army command, in this case it would be the General Staff. That it is not passed on to the General Staff? What is your opinion as a professional soldier? Is it possible that a report of this kind would not be sent on straight away, informing the General Staff of each and every incident that took place in the course of that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I can't answer for your Vojska Yugoslavia staff. I'm telling you the indications that General Dimitrijevic and General Perisic gave to me on several occasions which are itemised in my summary report. I would hope - sincerely hope - that there was a proper brief given back to your Vojska General Staff and to yourself as the Commander-in-Chief. I don't know that because I'm not privy to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But your assertions are, to put it mildly, strange. At least, they appear strange to me from the aspects of ethics and seem to be quite unbelievable. And at the end of this particular page - it is a long one with all the points - you talk about the discussion with Dimitrijevic on the 3rd of October, and you said that he said that General Pavkovic was trying to create a name for himself. Now, my question to you is based on this doubt, Mr. Crosland. I doubt that a general would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now having yet another speech. First of all, it doesn't matter what the evidence seems to you, it's what the witness said happened, and your views about it are totally irrelevant. Now, what is the question? You've asked something about General Pavkovic was trying to create name for himself. Did somebody say that to you, Colonel? Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. This came up in the two discussions on the 3rd of October and the 5th of November with my ambassador, that this was the feeling from members of the General Staff, that General Pavkovic was now acting outside the normal chain of command, direct back to Beograd and to Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. As I asked you this question as referring to professional soldiers, is it possible that there should not be reporting about each and everything that the army is doing in the field? Now, according to the rules of service and the provisions regulating the army's activities, it is duty-bound, even when it comes to sabotage, terrorist groups, and protection of borders and the protection of communication lines and the protection of itself and it is being shot at, do you really think that the commander of the rank of an army commander for each specific situation, concrete situation where soldiers are being shot at or when a border hut is being attacked at the border or a group is passing by that it actually has to ask the General Staff whether to proceed in keeping with its duties to protect the borders, to protect its unit, to protect the communication lines, to react against sabotage groups that it is -- that it has spotted, and only once it receives orders from the General Staff can it carry on in performing its duties. Is that what you're saying? Is that what you're assuming?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is completely untrue. I have never said or stated that a field commander should not act on his own initiative. Of course the commander of the 3rd Army from Nis, Colonel General Pavkovic, had to act on his own initiative. What was indicated by your General Staff at both CDS - chief of defence staff - and chief of counter-intelligence, was that it was outside their chain of command. They have to answer that question. I cannot answer that question. This was the feeling that they had, that they no longer, as chief of defence staff and as chief of counter-intelligence, had a control of what was going on in Kosovo. You must ask those three gentlemen concerned what they meant. They indicated to us General Pavkovic was acting directly to yourself on a different order of battle to what was going on in the chief of defence staff. That is the allegation. Of course a field commander has got the right and must have the right to react to the situation on the ground. And I never -- I've never gone against that feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it clear to you that his reactions, this reaction to the situation on the ground, is it clear to you that this reaction of his on the ground must be and was in conformity with the orders given down the chain of the command -- down the chain of command? It could not have been outside the chain of command, because in that case, he would have to bear the consequences because he has to report back about everything. And I maintain that General Pavkovic was not acting outside the chain of command, was not acting outside his own competencies and authorisations, regardless of the fact that you say that Dimitrijevic and Perisic told you that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Mr. Milosevic, then you and General Pavkovic must be responsible for what happened in Kosovo. And that included the destruction, massive destruction of civilian population and infrastructure around Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Crosland. Do you feel it to be probable - and that's why I'm asking you the question because I think it is impossible and quite improbable - that generals in the General Staff - you've mentioned the chief of the General Staff and the chief of the security service - should, with you - you were a foreigner, you were a colonel, a colonel of a foreign army - should talk to you about a colleague of theirs, the commander of the 3rd army of the Pristina Corps? Does that seem to you probable that he was doing this in order to make a name for himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you've missed the point. It's exactly what the witness said happened. It's no good your saying it doesn't seem probable. It's what happened, he says. If you say he's not telling the truth, of course you can put it to him, but there's no point saying it's not probable. It's what he said actually happened. Now, do you want to challenge it? You can. The witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, precisely because I consider this to be so improbable, I'm asking the witness whether he just conjured that up or maybe it was the impression he gained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am under oath, and I have written in several statements exactly what has happened. And on one occasion, on November the 5th, I think I'm correct in saying, there was also a meeting with General Dimitrijevic attended by my ambassador where this again was stated, that things were not as they should have been. And I suggest if you want to find out the answer, that you ask the gentleman concerned. But because of my good relationship with the Vojska Yugoslavia and what I had done for the Vojska Yugoslavia in helping to save the lives of six soldiers, during the evacuation from Kosovo I-49 Brigade out of Prizren, I got an accolade from General Simatovic for helping to withdraw that particular brigade and about 12.000 Serbs back to Strpce that may not have happened. So please do not accuse me of not looking after the aspects of the Vojska Yugoslavia. The welcome that I received when I went back to Belgrade in 2001 was a very generous welcome by your Vojska Yugoslavia General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Crosland. I assume that you're well acquainted with British military doctrine and you are a soldier of the British army, and that one of the elements, for example, is to protect dependent territories, regardless of the fact whether they are thousands of kilometres away. Now, your country, did it not deploy its own forces on countless occasions not only to fight terrorism but also to protect the dependent territories of its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's irrelevant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question is: How, then, can a member of that army consider that the Yugoslav army should not have taken part in the struggle against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have -- you have missed the point of the witness's evidence, which I've pointed out to you already and I will again. The point that he's made was that destruction caused by the use of artillery against villages, the point that he's made was the disproportionate response which was shown by your forces against the KLA. That's the point. It's been the point throughout this trial, and not one which you seem to have grasped.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I have grasped that essential point, and with the example of Prilep, which was highly fortified, it had walls of concrete, and it was built as a fortification in order to cut off the main communication line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you, as a soldier, do you consider that the deblocking and removal of such a fortification and stronghold which Prilep had been turned into can be done with infantry weapons, without the use of artillery? And how many victims and casualties should this cause, would this have caused? Speak as a professional soldier. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. The area of Prilep was a KLA stronghold, and your forces attacked it on many occasions when I was present in that area. Did they succeed in holding that area? No. Because you tactics were strong. And you can raze a village, as you did on many occasions, drive the population out, and within a matter of hours the population came back because they had nowhere else to go. The point I'm making is that your dispositions in Kosovo were totally inept and a very small number of terrorists initially - it grew later on - kept at bay a considerably larger number of forces. If they had been -- if they carried out operations in a far more professional way, I dare say the outcome would have been different. If you insist on going around, destroying everything that you suppose or your forces suppose is to do with the Kosovo Liberation Army, then your intelligence is not as good as it is meant to be. If you destroy the civilian population, inevitably you drive more people to support what was and is, and I have admitted, a terrorist organisation. We have had many, many incidents in Northern Ireland. We didn't go around destroying towns in Northern Ireland. The IRA probably destroyed more because of their bombing. And it's taken us 35 years to reach a partial, and I stress "partial," political initiative. What was totally lacking in Kosovo was any form of political initiative. As I've said, there was this air of revenge and never any reconciliation. And now Kosovo is still not part of Serbia. And there are many Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not pursue the future. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. Tell me this, because you mentioned Prilep: Does the opening of communication lines constitute a legitimate object, goal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I spoke to your General Staff. I asked Colonel General Vilickovic [phoen], who, sadly, was killed in Kosovo, why hadn't you opened the three channels of command across Kosovo, from Pec to Pristina, through Ribnik to Stimlje, Caraleva and Suva Reka, and he looked at me blankly and I had said, Well, they are not strong positions. How much more can I say? Correctly directed operations may, and I stress "may," have got you much better results than these completely wanton destruction of areas that achieved very little, because most of these areas came back under the Albanian influence very shortly afterwards as your troops withdrew to more static positions. I can't answer why they did that. That's something that you must ask your own generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that specific village, Prilep, Mr. Crosland, was emptied of the civilian -- of its civilian population and turned into a KLA stronghold, fortification, in order to block the main communication line. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I drove up and down the road from Djakovica to Decani, Pec more times than I care to remember, and I used to follow the beer truck that used to go around delivering beer to your positions, which was a great morale booster, and they were two very brave soldiers. Prilep definitely was a KLA area, and I've told you that several times. But razing it to the ground did nothing but actually harden the resistance in that area. And in the end, did you win that contest? I would suggest no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got beyond argument. Mr. Milosevic, you've got five minutes left and then you've had your time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Mr. May, that this kind of cross-examination of a witness that is claim -- presenting a mass of assertions, I cannot conduct this cross-examination in full within the time limits and time constraints you've given me. So I have no options but to use up the time I have. But this is an example of the fact that I have 50 more questions that I would like to ask this witness but won't have time to do so. But we'll have to deal with that separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Crosland, you are claiming that after the agreement which was reached between myself and Holbrooke, the army withdrew, in keeping with the agreement, and then two or three days later returned to its positions; right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's absolutely correct. And I was there when the three battle groups withdrew back to Prizren, Pristina, and Urosevac. And I actually informed the various powers that be that if we did not get people in place - KDOM or whatever it happened to be - then the KLA may well fill that vacuum. I issued that warning to various people. So I was aware of the very fluid situation in Kosovo at the time. I cannot be held responsible for what other people did. I reported, as my duty, as a professional soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. That's not what I'm asking you. That is not what I'm asking you. Until now, everybody established that we observed the agreement, that we diminished our own forces, withdrew our forces, and it is the first time that I hear this from you that we are tricksters who withdrew our troops and then returned them two or three days later. If it were so, why doesn't the Verification Mission say so in any one of its reports that we actually returned what we had withdrawn. And even General Naumann here claimed, in order to prove that we increased our presence, that we had, for example, 500 policemen more, which is about 5 per cent. Even that were correct, it would have constituted no more than 5 per cent. How can you claim that once we withdrew our forces, we returned them immediately behind the backs of the Verification Mission? Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's correct. Your Vojska Yugoslavia withdrew, as I've already indicated to you, quite correctly, back to their respective brigade barracks. The MUP, other elements, also withdrew. But within the next week or so, I myself saw many, many MUP returning on a roulement basis. Now, if the Kosovo Verification did not see that, it was perhaps because they were back in their bases. Some of us worked extremely long hours. And we're not silly, we know when people come back in and out using the cover of darkness. So perhaps the Kosovo Verification Mission did not see that. I can't answer for them. I am making a statement and I am confident and prepared under oath to say that the MUP were roulement in and out, came back in as just a large number very shortly after this. Your Vojska Yugoslavia did withdraw back, correctly, despite some attention from the Kosovo Liberation Army, to their barracks. And I have given them credit for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that it was the MUP precisely according to that agreement that had 10.024 of its own people in Kosovo at the time? Did you have the obligation to cooperate with the Verification Mission? Because there was the British KDOM, too. And also there were British verifiers in the Verification Mission. How come you did not draw the attention of the British verifiers and British KDOM to that? And that the fact that you have been claiming that the MUP returned after the agreement was signed is something that you didn't draw their attention to then. You are making this claim only now in 2002.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is completely untrue. The British KDOM were based in Prizren, which, as you know, is in the western side of Kosovo. The withdrawal of the MUP went out around the ring road of Pristina to Podujevo, and on to Nis, Prokuplje, et cetera, et cetera. They came back in through that route because we were based not far from Kosovo Polje, the obelisk there, in a house there. So that is where we saw these people come in and out. It was nothing to do with the British KDOM because they were not responsible for that area. People responsible were in the Pristina, Podujevo and eastern areas. Now whether they saw or did not see, I have no idea. That is there are job, not mine. But I made my reports back and they are stated in my reports as sworn evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this will be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was that? Was this my last question or am I supposed to put one more question to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, we've quoted here from the month of January a meeting that was held in London. It was your government with the participation of Secretary Cook and high officials, at which it was stated that most violations of the cease-fire were caused by the KLA.
