I assume Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that that was established in your reports as well. In your reports as well, not only in the reports of the Verification Mission, because I assume that your government receives information both from the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and also from verifiers as well. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course our government receives reports from all sorts of agencies. And the allegation that the majority of attacks were by Kosovo Liberation Army is possibly correct. What is -- that is respected. Unfortunately was the return of your forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need to pursue that part. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is no matter to assist the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you can be very quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded and you are free to go. And the Trial Chamber will adjourn for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, before we call the next witness, Dr. Baccard, who will be very brief, I wonder if I might raise a few administrative matters, some of which are somewhat urgent in the sense that they affect the witness after Dr. Baccard. In the first instance, I want to point out to the Court that the Prosecution intends to call Mr. Karleusa live, and I believe the Court has had an opportunity of seeing both his statement of that of Mr. Radojkovic, who we propose to call pursuant to Rule 92 bis, because, as you might be able to determine from their statements, the evidence overlaps and therefore could be part of the cumulative in nature. So I just want to alert the Court to our intention of proceeding in that way, if the Court approves. I also wanted to point out that Witness K32, you may have before you at the moment an application to have him proceeded with under Rule 92 bis. On reflection, that is a witness that I will be calling, and the subject nature of his evidence might be better if I were to call that evidence live. And again, that's for Your Honours to determine. Finally, and perhaps more urgently, after Dr. Baccard, who I think I'll take no more than 15 minutes with, on the list you have the next two witnesses, Merita Dedaj and Merfidete Selmani, and those witnesses we have requested to proceed with by way of Rule 92 bis, and thus far I'm not aware whether a ruling has in fact made its way to us, so I'm just asking about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ryneveld, there hasn't been a ruling because we didn't realise there was any plan to call these immediately. There's been a change in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm told that's true, Your Honour, and that's our fault and my apology. So it's as a result of us changing the order that it now requires the Court's permission for us to call them by way of 92 bis. So I'm not suggesting for a moment that the Court has been tardy in giving the ruling, it's just that, in order for us to be able to call them in that way, I wanted to alert you to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to consider that when we've heard Dr. Baccard's evidence. Let me deal with one other matter while we are awaiting the witness. We will approve the calling of Mr. Coo in chief before the recess, cross-examination after the recess. We have considered the statement of Mirjan Krasniqi, which was mentioned in evidence last Wednesday in connection with Suva Reka and during the evidence of Shyhrete Berisha. There was an application by the accused to exhibit the statement. The statement was marked for identification. The application now is to -- that it should be made part of the Prosecution case under Rule 92 bis. Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what I've said about the statement of Mirjan Krasniqi which you asked should be exhibited. There's now an application we're considering that it should be exhibited or it should be admitted, rather, under Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution have made that application. Do you want to say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know my general position that every witness should be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the usher is getting Dr. Baccard. There we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, thank you for coming back. There's no need to take the declaration because you're already under it, you having made it once already. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is getting directions, I might just alert the Trial Chamber to the location that this evidence refers to Cirez, which you will find at page 6 of the Kosovo Atlas number 2, and about dead centre in the page where you see on the left-hand side column there's a 5 and at the top there is a 90. Where those two intersect, about a half an inch to the right of the intersection of 5 and 90, you will see Cirez, C-i-r-e-z. That's the location that this evidence will be pertaining to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, at the conclusion of your evidence last day, you were asked to review the pathology reports carried out by the French team with respect to individuals found in three wells in the village of Cirez in Kosovo; is that correct? Sorry. I didn't get a response because the microphone wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I said yes. I said yes to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, sir, what information did you have available to you in order to review the autopsy reports and express an opinion at this courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: The material that I used that was given to me was -- is found in a binder called "Sexual assaults," with the reference number K1054, K1062, which include the analyses, report of Dominique Lecompte and Dr. Vorhauer as well as a scene examination report that was prepared by the team headed by a division head Mr. Dominique Gaillardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you show the witness a binder of material, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, Dr. Baccard, is this the binder that you indicate you were shown and does it contain the information you used in order to prepare your subsequent report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would tender that binder as an exhibit in these proceedings, if I may, Your Honour. Copies were -- were distributed earlier, but I believe last date they were handed up and returned. So I do need these -- this binder marked with an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 261.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, then, Doctor, very briefly, can you tell the Court what the subject matter of this autopsy report concerned? In other words, how many individuals and what were the circumstances to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: According to the documents that were given to me, we're talking about exhumations and autopsies that were carried out by the French forensic team on the 2nd and 3rd of July, 1998 -- 1999, rather, and there were eight female victims who were taken out of three wells. Four women were in well number 1, one was in well number 2, and three other women were in well number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, sir, in the autopsy reports, were these individuals given specific numbers? In other words, were they assigned particular numbers in order to keep the data straight?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Each of the victims was given a number, a code number with several letters; SI, which is representing Cirez, P for well - "puits" in French, "well" in English - the letter C for body, "corps" in French. The wells were numbered from 1 to 3 since there were three wells. SIP 1, 2 and 3. And the bodies were numbered from 1 to 4, which was the highest number of victims in 1, letters from C1 to C4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So just if I have it correctly, if you have a number such as SIP1C1, that would mean -- SIP1, would be -- that's the first well, and then the body would be C1. That would be the first body in the first well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. Now, sir, were the pathologists able to ascertain the ages of the individuals that were exhumed from these three wells?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. The age was determined. The victims were also identified by their relatives. The ages went from 18 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if you haven't already told us, the sex of the individuals in the wells? Were they all women?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. There were eight victims. They were all women.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, were the pathologists able to determine how long the bodies had been in the wells at the time they performed their exhumations on the 2nd and 3rd of July, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That estimate, which showed the amount of time that they were in the water, but it was approximate, the time that the forensic pathologists had was completely compatible with staying in water which would be for about two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So two and a half months, from early July, would be roughly what, mid-April 1999?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Approximately that, yes. I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did the autopsy determine a cause of death on any or all of these women?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: The cause of death which the French pathologist noted was the same for all the victims; that is, they were drowned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Drowned. Now, these -- to the best of your information and belief, these bodies were found in a well; is that correct? Or in a series of three wells.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you indicate, sir, that the symptoms were consistent with having been immersed in water for a period of time. So there was water in these wells?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear, if they died from drowning, does that mean that these -- what does that tell you about whether or not the victims were alive before they went into the well or not? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. And I mentioned this on page 2 of the addendum which I drafted on the 23rd of May, 2002. The conclusions of my colleagues, who were French pathologists, was that the cause of death was death through drowning. The report does not -- the autopsy does not specify whether additional examinations were carried out, but the observations that were made under microscopes were completely compatible with the death by drowning. So it is death -- well, that was -- those persons were drowned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge, was any attempt made to determine whether or not there had been evidence of sexual assault on any of the victims?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. That was systematically checked by the French pathologists. Obviously the state of preservation of the bodies represented an obstacle to bringing out the diagnosis. However, in two cases, it was possible for the experts to say, yes, that two of those victims had been subjected to sexual aggression. That is SIP1C1 and SIP1C2 which showed signs that were very, very clear that -- clearly indicated that there had been sexual attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself have an opportunity to study the photographs and the autopsy reports, and did you personally come to any conclusions about whether or not the autopsy reports were correct in their findings?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I myself examined the autopsy reports and the photograph albums. And in order to answer your question in respect of the two victims, in the first case the victim that is SIP1C1, we saw clinical signs associating the presence of red blood at the opening of the vulva and an abrasion-type lesion on the left thigh that pointed - I say pointed - to sexual assaults. Things were much clearer in respect of SIP1C2, because that victim also showed red blood at the vulva opening. She had lesions which showed traumatic violence on the upper third of the -- on the right thigh and the upper third of the left leg. And also, she was completely naked. That is, the lower half of her body was completely naked. And therefore, as regards that second case, the diagnosis showing sexual assault pointed more to that and could be considered as most probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, of the eight women exhumed from these wells, you say that there was an assessment that two had been sexually assaulted based on what you've just told us. Due to the state of putrefaction or decomposition of the other bodies, was it possible to make a determination whether or not they were not sexually assaulted? In other words, was it possible that they had been or could you rule it out?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: As I said, at first the state of preservation of the bodies, which showed putrefaction of the tissues and also a rather long amount of time spent in the water, made the experts' work difficult. And the lack of clinical signs, macroscopic clinical signs in the general sphere of the lower limbs showing traumatic lesions, the fact that those signs were not there does in no way eliminate the possibility of a diagnosis that there had been sexual assaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Finally, Doctor, you have provided a two-page report dated the 23rd of May, 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that report now be tendered as an exhibit, Your Honours? And once it is, I believe those will be my questions. Thank you. I might say, Your Honours, that I do not intend to show the witness the photographs. The binder that was marked as a previous exhibit refers, and if the Court wishes, I can perhaps indicate some of the photographs with numbers, but I don't propose to put them on the ELMO in respect of the witness -- the victims and their families.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you any questions for the witness related to the evidence which he's given about this report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baccard, do you know how far away the wells were from one another? Where the bodies were found, that is.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. In the reports of the crime scenes, I did see them. It was indicated there, but I can't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that the assertion is being made that the women whose bodies were found in the wells had been detained at a particular place? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. It does not deal with the report that I was asked to draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an expert, do you have any logical explanation as to why the bodies of these women were found in three separate locations, in three different wells?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I have no explanation in respect of the distribution of the victims into the three wells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know when the village from which these women were - as far as I can see, that's the village of Kozica - when it was free of the official state authorities, the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it occur to you that it would be necessary to establish that in view of ascertaining the time when you claim that these bodies were in these wells, in the water, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That point was not part of the expert mission that was given to me, the purpose of which was to check on the French pathologist expert reports and the crime scene analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know which party in the conflict did these bullet casings or shell casings of 105 millimetres belong to, the ones that were found near the wells in Cirez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not part of the witness's report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that in the addendum to the report it says that Mr. Baccard pointed out that he had studied the on-site investigation reports, and this was carried out by Dominique Gaillardon, if my pronunciation is correct, so it was included in the reports, and I can see by what is being distributed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not part of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how high the concrete wall of the well was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Which well are you talking about? That should appear in the crime scene analysis report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you bear in mind that, because it was your duty to view the scene itself in order to ascertain what had happened, how high is this wall? I see in some photographs it's made of concrete, in others, it's made of wood.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I was not to look -- I did not have the opportunity to look inside at the reports but, rather, look at the reports that had been drafted, so I limited myself to what was the mission that had been given to me. However, this appears in the expert report that Mr. Gaillardon prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Baccard. Only a short while ago, I got this binder with the photographs where these wells can be seen. So I've had much less time to look at this than you did, and I can see that the walls around the wells are either made of wood or of concrete and that they are quite high. And in these details, one can see that even on the edges of these walls, one could sustain injuries. So I'm asking you what kind of injuries can be sustained from the edges of these walls. Because you state what the injuries were like and the place where they did take place. I imagine that you had to be interested in that, how these edges could injure a person.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: In general terms, I would say that the type of wound that could be caused by a traumatism to the body from wood or concrete are usually superficial. They are usually abrasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said some kind of abrasions on the inner side of the upper part of the leg. Can these injuries be sustained when one jumps over such a fence? And we can see on the photographs that they are quite high and that the edge is pretty sharp.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: Each type of abrasion has to be looked at in respect of where it is. Its location on the inner side of the thigh could be possibly connected to other traumas. But when they appear in a -- along with other symptoms which show red blood and open orifices and the fact that the lower half of the body is naked, the interpretation becomes completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you exclude the possibility -- what I understood you to say was this, let's take it one by one: You concluded that those women drowned in the well; right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. I read the autopsy reports where my colleagues concluded that there had been death by drowning, and I judged that the comparison of the autopsy reports and the photographs was also compatible with this diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's water down there. But do you exclude the possibility, for example, of this kind: That the victim wanted to hide herself, that she jumped over the edge and that while she was jumping over these rough edges, these abrasions were caused, as you call them, on the inner side of her upper thigh and that, later on, she drowned; that nobody threw her there into the well. Would that be a theoretical possibility, plausible?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is possible to have that hypothesis, but that does not explain the red blood on the vulva, on the vulva opening, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know what the surface of the interior of the wall is, from the top to the surface of the water? Are there any -- any protrusions or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: According to the photographs that I saw, apparently there were kind of irregularities. There were some protrusions within side the -- on the inner part of the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what type of injuries can be caused from those protrusions? What injuries to the body with these rough edges?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That would depend on the size of the trauma that the body experiences when coming up against those rough spots. They could be skin abrasions or wounds, fractures. All would depend on the violence of the trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in view of the dimensions, the size that I can see on the photographs, I assume that you measured all this and that this was -- these were some very narrow wells. Not wide wells but narrow wells. So what injuries do you think this could cause to the body? Are they similar to the ones that you observed? Can this type of injury be incurred if an individual wanted to hide and had to jump over a well, even if a person wanted to commit suicide or anything else, but to jump there, could such injuries be sustained of the nature you've described or do you exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: As regards the relationship between the wounds and the well itself, that was studied and suggested by the autopsy report of the French expert. In one case there was the victim, SIP2C1, who had an injury to the scalp in the front part of the skull, and the experts noted also that within the well there were traces of blood on the wall of the well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on what parts of the body would these injuries be localised if, for example, the individual had jumped over this edge herself? Let us suppose that the person wanted to hide and jumped inside or was thrown inside, bearing in mind the width of the well, as we have seen, was narrow? Would these injuries differ in the latter case and in the former case?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That would depend on the position of the victim when she went into the well, whether she were to fall head-first or whether she was thrown in or whether she jumped in feet-first. As regards this case, there was a wound on the forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was the case with one of the victims, this injury to the forehead. Now, tell me this: The injuries on the bodies of these women, would they be more intensive than the ones you described had they been thrown into the well? Would they be more marked? Or like this particular case, the situation that I described to you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: As regards the lesions and the skin abrasions on the inner part of the thighs, it would be very unlikely that the lesions were caused by a fall, because since -- on the inner side of the thighs, this is an area which anatomically is protected when one falls into a narrow well. This also concerns the two victims for whom there is suspicions of sexual assaults. There were other traumatic lesions that were noted on five of the other victims, and they are fractures of ribs, which were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. caused before death. This concerns those victims who were mentioned at the bottom of the page of the report, the bottom of the first page, SIP1C1, SIP3, SIP3C2, SIP3C3. They had rib fractures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I asked you about this protected part of the body, as you called it, the inner thighs. Could those injuries have been sustained while jumping over the rough edges of the well? Because they weren't -- these parts of the body weren't protected because you put one foot forward, one leg forward, and then the other if you want to jump over.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: One has to understand that the state of the bodies did not allow us to have a very precise autopsy, given the putrefaction caused by how long they had been in the body [sic]. In fact, nothing allows us to eliminate the possibility that you've mentioned, but once again, that hypothesis does not allow us to explain the presence of blood at the vulva opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understood your understanding that it wasn't easy to establish whether they had in fact been sexually assaulted or not and so on, but as you're talking about blood, as you've just mentioned blood, could you answer this specific question: In the false environment such as the interior of a well -- moist environment, I'm sorry, does the hemolysis of erythrocytes take place, dissolving?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: In a moist environment, you have a humid, moist environment, you said that these bodies had been immersed in water for two and a half months, so in this kind of circumstance, in a wet, moist situation, does the hemolysis of erythrocytes take place or their dissolution. Dissolving, dissolution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does that mean in ordinary language? Can you help us, Dr. Baccard, as to what the accused means or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We're talking about a destruction of red globules. "Hemolysis" means the destruction of the red globules, corpuscles, rather, excuse me. And that phenomenon can occur, and in the report, it was made clear that the experts mention the presence of red blood, and we're not talking about any kind of liquid related to putrefaction but, rather, in respect of the other openings that showed mucous, like the mouth, there was no red blood, and that the red blood was only noted at the vulva opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my question is that this is a case of decomposition in this moist environment over a period of two and a half months. Now, my question is: Can you prove the origins of hemolysed blood, Dr. Baccard?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That could be possible with a microscopic analysis of the cells which appear in the blood, but I really don't see what the point of this question is. There was blood on the vulva opening. There was blood on the vulva opening. That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I apologise if I interrupted you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. No, no, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And tell me, after what period of time after death does the blood in the body lose its characteristics because of the decomposition and decay that sets in, and putrefaction, under the conditions in which these persons were to be found?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: It varies, and one cannot give a specific estimate. It depends on temperature, it depends on the type of water, it depends on the way the body is more or less protected by something. It's impossible to make a specific evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not possible to estimate this, make a specific estimate. And after what period of time is it not possible to ascertain the person's blood type?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That also depends on the state of preservation of the blood. If there's sampling under scientifically standard conditions, then it's possible for a long time. But everything depends on the condition of the blood that's been conserved or preserved, and it's very difficult to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, Dr. Baccard, what is decomposition fluid?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is a -- it's a phenomenon which is related to hemolysis and the destruction of tissue in the chest area, inside the thorax, or within the various body cavities. It's kind of a -- it's a mechanism which is involved in putrefaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had now more than 20 minutes with this witness. The Prosecution were quarter of an hour. You can have half an hour in total, which will give you rather less than ten minutes more with this witness. It is more than sufficient to cross-examine on this very narrow point, in the view of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could you tell me in advance, Mr. May, then, please? Because as far as I know, you have cut down my hour to 45 minutes, now you're cutting it down further to half an hour, as far as I can see. I've already mentioned once that pre-emption. I see that you can see in advance that I'm -- whether I'm going to ask a relevant or irrelevant question, what is allowed in cross-examination. I am not aware of the fact that this exists in court practice anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've got about seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Dr. Baccard, with bodies that have drowned and with decomposition and putrefaction set in, does the -- do the fluids ooze out, and in what part of the body does that take place, this loss of fluids and liquids?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: As I was saying, they would take place within the thoracic cavities, but also within the abdominal cavity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from the professional viewpoint, is it more correct to say that at the opening, vulva opening, if a woman is assumed to have been assaulted, whether there will be putrefactory liquid or blood present, what would you say, in view of the fact that the person had drowned?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: My colleagues, the pathologists, said this was not putrefaction that was coming but it was actually red blood. Ordinary blood which is putrefying has a kind of a blackish colour or a brownish colour to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, can you assess the fact that the blood was blood caused by sexual assault if the corpse has been immersed in water for two and a half months? Are you able to establish fresh or vivid red blood present or not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: The hypotheses which comes to one's mind when one sees this bright red blood at the vulva opening is that the victim, throughout the time that she was in the water, had her thighs closed against one another and that the vulva orifice was protected by the large lips and allowed avoiding of contamination by the water. That is what I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this: Is it completely reliable what you are stating? Is this something that represents a general -- generally accepted rule or is this merely a possibility from the aspects of your profession?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think that in this case I go back to what was said both by the French pathologists and what I put in the conclusion of my report. In light of the state of the bodies and the amount of time they were in the water, it was not possible to have an exact diagnosis. In one case, SIP1C1, the observations were compatible with the diagnosis of sexual assault; and for SIP1C2, the diagnosis seemed more than compatible and really pointed to various things. We cannot go further than that. All of this is related to the limits that are caused by how -- the state of preservation of the bodies. This is not an exact diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not an exact diagnosis then. Now, did I note this correctly when I looked through your report: None of the drowned women had any traces which would indicate that they fought against someone or that they were thrown forcibly or were injured as they were defending themselves in any way? None of this was noted on any of the bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's not correct. As I have already said, five of the victims showed rib fractures which were caused before death. One of them had a wound on the scalp. As regards the others, the lesions that were noted showing skin abrasions are described for victims SIP1C1 and SIP1C2. So they did show traumatic lesions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but is it logical that in the case of violent behaviour toward somebody that the injuries would be found on their hands and arms which the victim would use to defend him or herself or if they were forcibly detained or thrown into prison or thrown anywhere else? So did you detect any of these - how shall I say? - defence injuries, injuries sustained during a person's defence?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think that you didn't or you weren't able to look at the photographs of the bodies. The state of preservation of the bodies was very, very poor, and this once again is related to putrefaction and the amount of time that was spent in the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was looking at, precisely that. So the post-mortem on the bodies of these women, as far as I was able to see from the report, did not register any of these what we call protective or defence injuries which one would expect if somebody was forcibly thrown into a well. They would have sustained injuries while defending themselves. So how can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that. He's referred to the five cases of rib fractures. Now, one more question, Mr. Milosevic, and then that's the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your response to a question from Mr. Ryneveld when you said that there existed, although it was not easy to ascertain the assumption that the two victims had been sexually assaulted, is it possible to claim that the others were not sexually assaulted, raped? Although you said that it was very difficult to ascertain that in these two cases. And you said that you could not exclude that possibility. Now, can you explain that to us? Because what you're doing is with two victims, you say that the possibility existed but there was no probability or possibility with the other two. Now, what are your professional guidelines on the basis of which you say that this cannot be excluded with the other two bodies, where no possibility of that was established in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Recalled]
utterances.text: I repeat that as regards the two victims that I've spoken about, C1 and SIP1C2, the diagnosis of sexual assault was, for one of them, compatible with the signs found on the body, and for the other, highly probable. As regards the other victims, in light of the state of preservation, which was very poor, of the bodies, and the immersion for a long time in the water, the pathologists were not able to bring out microscopic signs which allow us to conclude with that diagnosis. But the absence of those signs does not allow us to exclude this type of assault in light of the fact that the bodies were extremely degraded and that preservation showed highly evolved tissue degradation which does not allow us to exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have nothing to ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will need to see these statements. We haven't got them with us. Can you give us some copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, Your Honour. Ms. Romano will be handling the next two witnesses, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will look at these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're considering now whether we should admit the statements of Merfidete Selmani and Merita Dedaj under Rule 92 bis. Before we decide, it's right that you should have the opportunity to make any objection you wish to. We note your general objection that all evidence should be given verbally and not by written form. We've heard that. Is there anything else you'd like to add in these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure I'm clear on what you're asking me, but as you say, you know my general objection and you do whatever you like anyway, I don't see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit them subject to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness we'll be calling is Merita Dedaj, the first one. And, Your Honours, I also point out that the villages that the witness will be mentioning, and it's mentioned in her statement, are located on page 9 and 10 of the atlas. It's right in the middle. It is in the Gjakove area. And it refers to villages such as Meja, Korenica, Guska, Babaj. They're all in the middle of the page, both pages. While we wait for the witness, Your Honours, I also would like to inform the Court that the witness this morning brought with her several photos, and we reviewed the photographs with her, and we selected I think approximately four or five photos. I have copies in black and white here, and I suggest or, with the permission of the Court, that I put the photos on the ELMO and I explain what the photos are and the Court makes a decision about the admissibility as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please give your first and last name to the Court. I will repeat the question. Can you please give your first and last name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Merita Dedaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you born on 8 January, 1983? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you born in Guska in the Gjakove municipality?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 8 April 2000?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And on 12 July of this year, did you attend a meeting with an officer from the Registrar of this Tribunal, and did you review your statement and did you make an addendum of your statement to clarify and correct some dates? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, did you confirm that the contents of your statement are correct and true?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Might the statement and addendum be tendered into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let it have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 263, the original, and 263A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is from Guska village, Gjakove municipality. She was 16 years old and still attending school in 1999 and lived with her parents, one sister, and three brothers. She witnessed the killing of nine males on 27 April 1999. Amongst these men were her father, uncle, and cousin. Serbian forces controlled the area where the witness lived from autumn 1998. VJ and police constantly patrolled the area, which is close to the Albanian border. On 29 March 1999, VJ forces led by Dragan, one of the VJ commanders, expelled the witness and other villagers from Guska, giving them one hour to leave. The villagers headed for Korenica and en route they were escorted by VJ vehicles. On arrival in Korenica, the witness stayed in a field with other displaced persons. She stayed there for one week. A week later, the displaced persons left in a convoy numbering 1.000 people. On arrival at Orize, the convoy stopped and people were ordered to return to Korenica. The witness describes the atmosphere of fear created by the Serb forces. On 27 April 1999, at 6.30 a.m., the VJ forced entry into the house where the witness was staying. The occupants were ordered out of the house. The men were beaten and robbed, and the women and children were separated from the men and ordered to leave. As they left, the women and children were made to make the Chetnik sign and shout "Serbia." The witness saw her father, uncle, a cousin, and five other men being lined up against the wall of the house. From a distance of approximately 20 metres, she heard multiple shots lasting two minutes. On turning back, she saw the men falling to the ground. The witness could not judge whether these men were dead, but none of them were seen again, and they are all listed as missing persons by the ICRC, International Committee of the Red Cross. As the witness left Korenica, she heard gunfire and saw houses burning. The witness and others formed a convoy and walked towards Djakovica. En route, she saw two unidentified dead bodies covered with blankets being placed on a VJ truck by soldiers. The convoy was ordered to follow the truck. On arrival at Bishtazin, the convoy was stopped at a checkpoint. Serb police abducted a number of men from the convoy, most of whom have not been seen since. The witness and her relatives sheltered in the village until the end of the war. On returning to her village, the witness saw that her house had been ransacked and looted and the cattle had been killed. Gjon Dedaj, her uncle, took several photographs of both her family home and the home of Pjeter Dedaj. If the usher could show the witness or put on the ELMO the photographs in this order. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, the first photograph is of your house taken by your uncle when you returned to Kosovo. It shows damage to the interior. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. It's here. That's my house which was ravaged, ransacked. This is right after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. The second photo, please. This is a photograph of Pjeter Dedaj's house, and also taken after the return to Kosovo, showing the damage. Pjeter is your uncle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. The third photo. That photo, Witness, shows uniforms left by the Serb forces in the house of Pjeter Dedaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Have you also seen the interior of the house, and have you also seen these uniforms that are depicted in the photo?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've seen them. I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The other photo, please. Is this the same house of Pjeter Dedaj, and it also shows the uniforms left by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution submits the photos into evidence. And I have copies here with me. They are black and white, due to the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 264.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Have you got questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that you gave a statement to the investigators of the International Crisis Group and then to the investigators of this institution. How were you in a position to give a statement to the investigators of the International Crisis Group and then to the investigators of this institution here?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Of course I was able. I came back after the war, and they came, and I was in a position to give them a statement about what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how old were you when you gave your statement first to the investigators of the International Crisis Group and then to these investigators from here?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: I was 16. It was right after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you give all your statements in the presence of your mother or not?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: No. I was alone at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your mother and your aunt, did they give any statements to the mentioned investigators?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the two of them were with you all the time; right? During the period that you describe in your statement, that is.

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your mother and your aunt, were they with you all the time during these events that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they did not make any statements.

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would first like to remind you of page 1 of the statement -- or, rather, it's page 2. You say: "The Serb forces, the VJ, and police were deployed in our area from autumn 1998. This is an area near the border, as they were constantly patrolling this area. As far as I can remember, there were no incidents between Serbian forces and villagers in that period. In that period of time, I did not see any paramilitary units in our area. I used to go to school, to Gjakove every day on foot, and I never had any problems with the police checkpoint that had been set up in Brekovac. Only once they addressed me by saying that I had to greet them." Later, you say that you went to Korenica, and you say that during that week, you did not see a single crime that had been committed there. And now let's go back to the beginning. You continue by saying that: "On the 24th of March, 1999, the NATO airstrikes against Serbia started. From that day, my family and I could not go out any more." And now my question is the following: From the 24th of March, when the NATO airstrikes began against Serbia, why could you and your family not go out any more?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: We didn't dare to go out because the police had a checkpoint there. They were everywhere. And they would take all the men away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim on the same page and in the same paragraph that the army forces, on the 25th of March, went to the villages of Deve and Babaj, and you say that they executed eight civilian men there. How do you know that? You were not there. How do you know that they killed eight men there?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Because the commander of the army, called Nikola Micunovic, also known as Dragan, came to my uncle's house and told him to go and bury the eight dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you found out from your uncle or from your uncles that he buried eight bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could he tell you, because he was asked to bury them, how these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people got killed?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: No. He didn't know how they had been killed. He just knew that they had been killed and he was told to go bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard about these people from him, and he did not know how they got killed. Why do you then say that it was the army that killed them? On the basis of what did you infer that it was the army that killed them?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: The army commander was the one who came. And there were two other soldiers with him who called my uncle and told him to go and bury the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But my question pertains to something else. I understand that he called your uncles to go bury the dead there, but on the basis of what did you conclude that the dead people got killed by the army?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Well, it was well-known that the soldiers killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand that. How did you know that it was the army that killed them? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: That's what -- that's what my uncle said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But your uncle went there to bury them. So he went there when they were already dead and when the commander asked him to go and bury them. How could he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness has said, what the witness has said is that it was well-known that that is what happened and that her uncle told her. Now, she can't take it any further than that. That's what her uncle told her and that must be the extent of her evidence. It's now quarter to, and we will have to adjourn. Ms. Dedaj, we have to adjourn for the day now because there's another case that's got to come into this courtroom. So I'm afraid I must ask you to come back tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence. Would you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning, and would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, then, at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of July, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
